Short-eared sengis (Macroscelides proboscideus) exhibit a life-history profile that aligns closely with their small-bodied, insectivorous lifestyle in the arid regions of southern Africa. Field studies indicate that gestation in this species, measured under typical active body temperatures of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], lasts approximately 60.5 days [tg = approximately 60.5 days], a duration that is relatively protracted for a mammal of its size and likely reflects the highly precocial developmental state of the neonates at parturition. Newborn pups weigh roughly 8 grams [Wwb = roughly 8 grams] at birth, a value that constitutes a considerable proportion of the mother's own body mass and underscores the substantial maternal investment required during pregnancy. The gestation period is consistent with records for other macroscelidids, which tend to have longer pregnancies compared with similarly sized rodents, a pattern often attributed to the advanced state of neuromuscular development observed in sengi offspring.

Following birth, the neonatal sengi enters a period of rapid growth and sensory maturation while remaining dependent on the mother's milk. The time since birth at weaning is typically around 20 days [tx = around 20 days] when maintained at a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], although some individual variation has been reported, with weaning observed as early as 16 days or as late as 25 days in captive colonies. By the time of nutritional independence, the young have accumulated considerable mass. Measurements from a captive breeding population show that the wet weight at weaning is approximately 22 grams [Wwx = approximately 22 grams], representing a nearly threefold increase over the birth weight. This period of milk-dependence is brief compared to many altricial rodents, reflecting the sengi's precocial trajectory and the energetic pressures of an unpredictable desert environment where rapid development is advantageous.

Sexual maturation proceeds rapidly after weaning, with individuals becoming capable of reproduction at a young age. The time since birth at puberty is approximately 43 days [tp = approximately 43 days] when recorded at the species' typical active body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], though published accounts note a range of 41 to 45 days in well-nourished captive individuals. This early onset of reproductive maturity is a hallmark of a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid turnover, particularly in response to seasonally pulsed resource availability in the Namib and Karoo ecosystems. Upon reaching adulthood, males and females differ slightly in their ultimate body dimensions. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 40 grams [Wwi = approximately 40 grams], while males attain a slightly greater mass of about 42 grams [Wwi = about 42 grams]. This modest sexual dimorphism in body mass is common among sengis and may relate to differences in intrasexual competition or dispersal behavior.

The species' reproductive output reflects its capacity to capitalize on favorable environmental conditions. Female short-eared sengis can produce multiple litters within a single breeding season when resources are abundant. Data from captive studies indicate that females give birth to litters of 1 to 2 pups [N_R_i = litters of 1 to 2 pups] per reproductive event, and under optimal conditions they may produce up to 5 such litters per year [F_R_i = up to 5 such litters per year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive output. The overall body length, measured from the tip of the nose to the end of the tail, reaches an ultimate nose-tail length of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters] in fully grown adults. This compact size is typical of the genus Macroscelides and is well-suited for maneuvering through the dense shrub and grasses of their semi-desert habitat. The combination of moderate litter sizes, high potential litter frequency, and a small body plan reflects an adaptive balance between fecundity and the energetic constraints of an arid environment.

Longevity records for short-eared sengis, derived from both field mark-recapture studies and captive maintenance, indicate a modest maximum lifespan. Documented individuals have been recorded living up to 8 years [am = up to 8 years] under the stable conditions of captivity at a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], though wild individuals likely experience a shorter average lifespan due to predation and environmental stochasticity. This lifespan is comparatively long for a mammal of such small size, a feature that may be linked to their low basal metabolic rate and relatively low predation pressure in their sparsely vegetated habitats. From a broader ecological perspective, the life-history syndrome of M. proboscideus — characterized by a long gestation for a small mammal, precocial neonates, early weaning, rapid sexual maturity, and a moderately extended lifespan — positions the species as a classic example of a slow-paced, bet-hedging strategist adapted to the unpredictable rainfall and resource pulses of the Succulent Karoo biome. This multifaceted suite of traits underscores how the ecology of the arid zone has shaped the temporal organization of growth, reproduction, and survival in this distinctive afrotherian lineage.
